processing: Fully oxidised 'new-style' Keemun: tender spring leaf is withered, rolled, oxidised and then hand-shaped in a warm pan into tight spirals before final drying, so the whole leaf curls like a snail instead of being cut.
harvest_season: Early spring, from around Qingming to Guyu (April), a bud with one or two leaves; the shaping needs tender, pliable leaf.
appearance_dry: Tight, glossy dark spirals the size of a fingernail, curled like small snails and flecked with golden tips.
appearance_wet: The spirals unwind into whole, tender copper-red leaves with buds.
taste_profile: Lifted rose and orchid florals over honey and cocoa, with a sweet, soft body and the 'Qimen fragrance' pushed forward by the shaping.

brewing.notes: Water around 90 °C and a slightly longer second steep while the spirals open; a glass pitcher shows them unwinding. Western-style: 3 g per 250 ml, 3 minutes, neat.

vintage_note: Sold as the current year's spring harvest, usually with the picking window stated; the florals that justify the price fade within a year, so buy the fresh lot each spring. Not an ageing tea.
description:
Keemun Xiang Luo, 'fragrant snail', is the youngest of the Keemun styles: a whole-leaf spring Keemun hand-rolled into tight spirals, developed in the late 1990s when Qimen makers started chasing the premium loose-leaf market instead of the export blends. Together with Keemun Jin Zhen, the straight 'golden needle' version made the same way, it belongs to what the county calls new-style Keemun – same leaf, same oxidation, new shapes.

The leaf is tender spring picking from the local small-leaf bushes, withered, rolled and oxidised like any Keemun, and then shaped by hand in a warm pan: the oxidised leaf is rolled and pressed into spirals as it dries, a technique borrowed from the green tea Bi Luo Chun. The shaping bruises the leaf a little more and concentrates aroma, which is why Xiang Luo is the most floral of the Keemuns, and the whole, curled leaf extracts slowly, which keeps the cup soft.

Expect rose and orchid up front, honey and cocoa underneath, a sweet, round body and a long floral finish over six or seven steeps; the second steep is the best, once the spirals have opened. Water around 90 °C and short infusions suit it; too hot and the florals turn sharp, too long and the honey goes tannic. It is a neat-drinking tea and a good one to brew in glass.

It is sold as the current spring, priced above gongfu and Mao Feng from the same maker because of the hand work, and the shape makes it easy to judge: spirals should be tight, glossy and even with visible golden tips, and should smell of roses and cocoa. Loose, flat or dusty leaf means poor shaping or old stock. Check the label says Qimen; the shape is easy to copy on leaf from anywhere.

If you already like Keemun Mao Feng, this is the next step up in aroma, and tasting the two together shows how much a shape can do.
sources_note: Development of Xiang Luo and Jin Zhen as 'new-style Keemun' in the late 1990s follows Chinese trade and research accounts; the exact year and originator vary by source.
